title: The AI comeback: three enablers that converged
summary: Why AI accelerated after 2012: Big Data, GPUs and deep learning converging, the people behind each, AlexNet's ImageNet result, and what this means for judging a firm's AI readiness.

chunks.heading: Not one breakthrough, but three converging enablers
chunks.explanation_md:
AI's dramatic acceleration **after 2012** was **not one breakthrough insight**. It came from **three separate technological trends converging at the same moment**, each pioneered by identifiable people and institutions, and each **necessary but not sufficient on its own**.

| Enabler | Pioneers | Role in the comeback |
|---|---|---|
| **Big Data** | **Jeff Dean & Sanjay Ghemawat (Google)**, and the wave of large internet platforms, Google, Facebook and Amazon among them | Built infrastructure to process massive datasets and generated huge volumes of user data from roughly **2000** onward; **cloud platforms** made large-scale storage and distributed computing affordable. AI finally had **enough raw material to learn from** |
| **GPUs** | **Ian Buck (NVIDIA, launched CUDA in 2006)** | **CUDA** let researchers write general-purpose programs on graphics hardware, making GPUs a computing engine roughly **100x faster than CPUs** for neural-network training, cutting training from **weeks to days or hours** |
| **Deep Learning** | **Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio**, the "Godfathers of Deep Learning", joint recipients of the **2018 Turing Award** | Advanced the architectures and training techniques (CNNs, sequence models, optimisation methods) that let deep networks learn from the new data and hardware, culminating in **AlexNet** by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton in **2012** |

chunks.heading: AlexNet 2012: synergy is the lesson
chunks.explanation_md:
The chapter says the **synergy**, not any single part, is the managerial lesson.

**AlexNet's 2012 win** in the **ImageNet** competition: a **top-5 error rate of just 15.3%**, roughly **10.8 percentage points** better than the runner-up's **26.2%**.

Note: the slide prints roughly 10.8 points; 26.2 minus 15.3 is 10.9.

**What "top-5" means:** the correct label appeared among the model's **five most likely predictions**, a standard and generous measure for a **1,000-category task**. It is **not** a claim that AlexNet was right **85%** of the time on its single best guess.

The win depended **simultaneously** on:
- **deep convolutional networks** (the **algorithm**),
- **large labelled datasets** (the **fuel**),
- **GPU acceleration** (the **engine**).

Remove any one of the three and the breakthrough **does not happen on the same timeline**.

key_terms.meaning: The share of cases where the correct label was not among the model's five most likely predictions.

chunks.heading: Assessing AI readiness today
chunks.explanation_md:
The same logic applies to a **firm's own AI readiness** today: **data, compute and algorithmic capability must be assessed together**, not as independent checkboxes.

The chapter's executive takeaway: the post-2012 comeback rested on **three converging enablers, Big Data, GPUs and Deep Learning algorithms**, pioneered by named people and institutions, and readiness should still be judged **against all three, not any one in isolation**.

Reflection question: of the three enablers, which is your own organisation strongest in, and which is the **binding constraint** on its AI ambitions?
chunks.exam_line: Judge AI readiness on data, compute and algorithms together, never one in isolation.
